title: Resurrection at the Time of the End
summary: At the time of the end, Michael will arise, a time of unmatched distress will come, and God's people whose names are written in the book will be delivered. Many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting contempt, and the wise will shine like the stars. Daniel is told to seal the book; when he asks how long and what the outcome will be, he receives cryptic numbers and a personal promise that he will rest and rise to his inheritance at the end of the days.
story: This chapter completes the final vision (chapters 10 to 12) and closes the book. Chapter 11 ended with a persecuting king who magnifies himself and then falls. The question left hanging is what becomes of those who died faithful under him, the wise who fell by sword and flame (11:33-35). Chapter 12 answers: death will not have the last word. The book that began with young Daniel taken captive to Babylon ends with old Daniel told to go his way and rest, with a promise that he too will rise. The hope that has run through Daniel, that God's kingdom will outlast all the kingdoms of the earth, now reaches beyond history to the resurrection of the dead.
historical:
On the critical dating, the chapter was written for Jews suffering under Antiochus IV between 167 and 164 BC, when the temple's daily sacrifice had been stopped and many faithful people had been killed. For them, the promise of resurrection answered the most painful question of the persecution: whether those who died for the law had lost everything. The same hope appears in 2 Maccabees 7, where a mother and her seven sons die under torture confident that God will raise them. On the traditional dating, the chapter was revealed to Daniel in the Persian period, about 536 BC, as a promise for God's people in the crisis still to come and at the end of history.

The numbers in verses 7, 11, and 12 have been read in several ways. A time, times, and half a time (also in 7:25) is usually understood as three and a half years or periods, half of seven, a broken and limited span. The 1,290 and 1,335 days are both a little more than three and a half years. Critical scholars often suggest they reflect successive adjustments as the end was awaited, or symbolic figures. Those who apply them to the Maccabean period note that the temple was rededicated in December 164 BC, about three years after its desecration. Futurist interpreters see the extra days as periods of judgment and preparation after a future tribulation. Many interpreters of all views hold that the point is not a timetable but assurance that the suffering has a fixed limit, known to God.
cultural:
Most of the Old Testament speaks of death as going down to Sheol, the shadowy realm of the dead, and says little about life beyond it. There are hints of more: God's power over death (1 Samuel 2:6), the hope of being taken to God (Psalm 49:15; 73:24), and Isaiah's promise that the dead will live and their bodies rise (Isaiah 26:19). Ezekiel's valley of dry bones (Ezekiel 37) used resurrection as a picture of national restoration. Daniel 12:2 is the clearest statement in the Old Testament of a bodily resurrection of individuals, and the only one that speaks of a resurrection to judgment as well as to life. The image of sleeping in the dust recalls Genesis 3:19, where humans return to the dust from which they were taken; here the dust gives them back.

The book of life, in which names are written, draws on the ancient practice of keeping registers of citizens (Isaiah 4:3; Psalm 69:28; Malachi 3:16). Sealing a book meant closing and authenticating a document so it could be opened later by the right person, like a legal deed stored for the future (Jeremiah 32:9-14). The oath with raised hands (verse 7) is the most solemn form of oath, sworn by the God who lives forever.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1-4 are the climax of the messenger's revelation that began in 11:2, written in elevated poetry. Verses 5-13 are an epilogue that returns to the setting of chapter 10: the river, the man in linen, two further figures on the banks, and Daniel as a bewildered questioner. The two questions of the epilogue (how long, and what will be the outcome) are the questions of every suffering believer. The answers are deliberately partial. The words are closed up and sealed; the wise will understand, but even Daniel does not. The book ends not with a full explanation but with a pastoral word to one man: go your way, rest, and rise. The phrase at the end of the days frames the close, matching the latter days of 10:14.

outline.t: Deliverance, resurrection, and the shining of the wise
Seal the book until the time of the end
How long? A time, times, and half a time
What will be the outcome? The wise will understand

doctrines.note: The chapter's hope is resurrection: many who sleep in the dust will awake. The faithful who died under persecution are not lost, and Daniel himself is promised that he will rise to his inheritance. This is the Old Testament's clearest anticipation of the Christian hope of the resurrection of the body.

Resurrection is not only to life but also to shame and everlasting contempt (verse 2). History moves toward a final judgment in which faithfulness and wickedness are made plain, and the wise who led many to righteousness are honored.
The numbers of days, however they are read, place a limit on the time of distress. The suffering of God's people is measured, known, and bounded by him.

The wise understand and teach, and they will shine like the brightness of the heavens. In Daniel, wisdom is faithful understanding of God's purposes that leads others to righteousness, not cleverness or secret calculation.

words.note: Yashen, sleeping. Sleep is a common biblical image for death, but here the image points forward: sleepers awake. The New Testament uses the same picture, speaking of believers who have fallen asleep and will be raised (1 Thessalonians 4:13-16).

Olam, a long age, everlasting. Everlasting life and everlasting contempt appear side by side in verse 2, and the phrase everlasting life occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. The same word describes God, who lives forever (verse 7), so the life promised shares in his own endurance.

Deraon, abhorrence or contempt. It appears only here and in Isaiah 66:24, the last verse of Isaiah, which describes the dead bodies of those who rebelled against God as loathsome to all. Daniel draws on Isaiah's final picture of judgment.

Goral, lot, the stone or token used to allot shares of land when Israel entered Canaan (Joshua 18 to 19), and so the share itself. Daniel is promised that he will rise to his inheritance, his allotted portion, at the end of the days. The exile who never returned to the land is promised a share in God's final kingdom.

christ: Jesus spoke of the resurrection in Daniel's terms: the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment (John 5:28-29). He also used Daniel's language of an unparalleled time of distress (Matthew 24:21) and pictured the righteous shining like the sun in their Father's kingdom (Matthew 13:43), echoing verse 3. What Daniel saw at the end of history, the New Testament proclaims has already begun: Christ has been raised from the dead as the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20). The bodily resurrection of Jesus is the church's confession and the guarantee that Daniel's promise will be kept. Christians have also heard in the phrase those who lead many to righteousness an echo of the servant of Isaiah 53:11, who makes many righteous, a role the New Testament gives to Christ.

hard.q: Does many who sleep mean that only some will be raised?
hard.a:
Verse 2 says many who sleep in the dust will awake, not all. Some interpreters take the verse at face value as a limited resurrection: in context, the persecution of chapter 11 produced both martyrs and traitors, and God raises the faithful to vindicate them and the apostates to judge them. On this view Daniel is not yet teaching a general resurrection of all humanity, which later revelation makes clear.

Others note that many in Hebrew can carry an inclusive sense, the many as opposed to the few, as in Isaiah 53:11-12, and that the verse describes a resurrection of two groups that together cover everyone. Jesus' words in John 5:28-29, which speak of all who are in the tombs and divide them into the same two destinies, suggest that he read Daniel as describing the general resurrection. Either way, the chapter's teaching is clear on its main points: the dead will be raised bodily, the resurrection leads to two different ends, and the faithful who died under persecution will be vindicated. Christians confess the resurrection of the body and the life everlasting as first-order truths; how much Daniel 12 by itself teaches about their scope is a question on which careful readers differ.

questions: Daniel's first readers had watched faithful friends die. How does the promise of bodily resurrection change the way you think about those who have died in faith?
Daniel is not told everything he wants to know, only to go his way and rest. How do you live faithfully with unanswered questions about the future?
Those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars. Who has done that for you, and whom might you lead?
